# **Canonical copy style guide**

## About this guide

This is the Canonical copy style guide — the source of truth for voice, tone, grammar, formatting, and naming conventions used across all Canonical communications.

## Overview

The purpose of this style guide is to build your confidence in writing and help everyone at Canonical write consistently across the organization. While there is a lot of detail, including words and phrases to avoid and common style errors, there are a few general points to remember:

* Keep it simple and concise
* Assume nothing
* Be consistent
* If you don't know, ask

## Writing about Canonical and our products

Business doesn’t mean boring. Personalization stands at the heart of Ubuntu and the personal touch is also part of what makes Canonical different. We are friendly experts, approachable and straight-talking. We are human and we write for humans. That’s part of our promise. Whether you’re talking to a CEO or a CIO, a systems administrator or a consumer, there’s no need to lose your personality in the process. It’s part of what makes you, and Canonical, special.

## Brand voice

**We are authoritative, but not arrogant.**

Open source can be complex, and we take care to explain it in a way that’s direct and straightforward. We strive to be thought leaders in the industry, but we know that everyone isn’t an expert.

* We provide accurate, honest, truthful information to our audience.
* We convey a deep understanding of our sector.
* We highlight our team members and the expertise they bring to the company.
* When we write for non-technical users, we use industry jargon sparingly and are always mindful to provide explanations when we use terms that may be unfamiliar.

**We are precise, but not pedantic.**

Our messaging is clear and to the point without being intimidating. We value clarity and accuracy, and stay away from unnecessary complexity.

* We say what we mean using specific, accurate language.
* We keep our language clear and concise, and avoid overly convoluted sentences.
* We prioritize the most important information and present it in a clear, easy-to-read manner.
* We use subheadings, visuals, bullet points and lists to make our messaging easy for our audience to read and digest.

**We are approachable, but not shallow.**

Our products are designed to be elegantly simple, our communications are just as accessible. We pride ourselves on being approachable experts, able to bridge the gap between technical complexity and customers of all skill levels. At the same time, we strive to communicate with depth and expertise. Our materials are not shallow or superficial.

* We strive to be a trusted resource for technical and non-technical users alike.

* We use everyday examples, illustrations, and stories to make our messaging relatable.

* We use visuals and multimedia to make complex topics easier to understand.

* We use both technical and non-technical language to craft messaging that’s appropriate for a wide audience.

**We are confident, witty and playful.**

We’re passionate about the work we do and the contributions we’ve made to the open source community. We’re not afraid to make opinionated decisions that challenge the status quo. At the same time, we strive to lift up others and we admit our mistakes when we’re wrong.

* We communicate our choices and decisions in a respectful and confident manner, and we stand by them.
* We use storytelling to showcase the positive impact our products have had for our customers.
* We use a positive, witty and playful tone in our messaging.
* We actively work to promote the value and benefits of open source.

### Brand voice summary

* Canonical’s brand voice is the voice of a friendly expert – confident and authoritative, but approachable.
* We use concise, action-oriented language, and we build trust with readers by sharing expert insights and highlighting data.
* We are witty and playful.

## Sentence length

The average sentence length in any document should be between 12 and 20 words. Not longer.

## Tone

Expert, witty, precise, relatable, clear.

## Readability

Readability targets are based on the Flesch-Kincaid scale. Email and website copy: approximately Grade 7. Articles, ebooks, and whitepapers: approximately Grade 12.

## AI writing guidelines

This style guide is the source of truth for all Canonical copy. When writing on behalf of Canonical, apply these guidelines consistently to ensure output matches the brand voice, tone, and conventions defined here.

All AI-assisted content must read as though written by a human expert — not as generic LLM output. Avoid filler phrases, hedging language, and over-formal constructions. When in doubt, refer to the brand voice and words-to-avoid sections.

## Inclusive language

Language changes over time and so we need to keep learning and improving how we communicate. Inclusive language supports our users and our mission of making open source software and products accessible for our entire community.

We want to choose words that respect and value difference, and avoid words that exclude and divide. Writing inclusively may take some practice, and that’s ok. You can always ask questions.

There are certain categories of words to avoid, for example:

* Do not use gendered pronouns. Use ‘they/them’ instead.
* Do not use ableist words like ‘see’ or ‘hear.’ Instead, use ‘explore’, ‘access’, or ‘learn more’.
* Find alternatives for words with racist or misogynist origins. For example, instead of ‘middleman’ and ‘outmanned,’ use ‘middle person’ and ‘under-resourced’.

## Security claims, hyperbolic and absolute statements

When communicating about our products and services, we should take special care not to use hyperbolic language, make absolute statements or claims that cannot be backed up.

For example, “Secure open source,” makes a claim that the source code is free from vulnerabilities. This is impossible to prove, and also unlikely. Even with the best of processes, it is generally considered a certainty that software will have vulnerabilities discovered during its lifetime.

It is important that any Canonical official material (such as our website, marketing material, contracts) only make accurate, and provable security claims.

**Avoid**:

* Secure open source software
* Most secure operating system
* Security-guaranteed
* Always secure
* Fully secured supply chain

* Game-changing

* Revolutionary

**Use instead**:

* Trusted open source
* Designed with security in mind
* Security-maintained
* Maintained
* Supported
* We help you secure your open source supply chain
* Automated security patching/maintenance

## Conventions

To help make our writing recognizable, we also follow a set of rules or conventions.

### Use US spelling

We are a global, remote-first company and although we have a head office in the United Kingdom, most of our audience is in the US. Until recently, we used UK English in our communications but given our growing business and audience in North America, we decided to adopt US English in external communications. Please note: we will take a staged approach to this change. There is no need to retroactively change all your content.

*Snapshots of our audience demographics for Ubuntu.com and canonical.com between January 1 - August 1, 2024*

Outside of the website and when communicating with a local audience, content should be adapted to local English or any other language, as appropriate.

Frequent mix-ups include:

| US English | UK English |
| :---- | :---- |
| license (verb) | license (verb) |
| license (noun) | licence (noun) |
| defense (noun) | defence (noun) |
| sausages, beans, and mash | sausages, beans and mash |
| program (TV, agenda) | programme (TV, agenda) |
| program (IT) | program (IT) |
| percent | per cent |
| Data center | Data centre |
| skeptical | sceptical |
| catalog | catalogue |
| traveling | travelling |
| -able | -eable |
| -ize | -ise |
| -or | -our |

### Using the term “open source”

How to write “open source'' is always going to be a point of contention. However, in an effort to ensure consistency across Canonical, we're opting for the grammatically correct approach as defined below.

Only capitalize the term “open source” when it's part of a name. For example:

* Open Source Initiative
* Open Source Definition

Otherwise, please use lower case and two words. For example:

* We believe open source is the way forward.
* I love open source.

Do not hyphenate open source.

### Naming conventions for our products and services

#### **Ubuntu**

It can be easy to get in a muddle when referring to different Ubuntu products and services. If you're not sure how something should be described, check with the relevant product or service owner, or a member of the marketing team.

* Ubuntu should be referred to as “Ubuntu,” not “Ubuntu Linux.”
* Ubuntu is used in “countries,” not “markets.”
* Ubuntu is written with a capital U.
* Ubuntu is both a project and a product. Be clear about which one you mean.

#### **Ubuntu release names**

When referring to a specific release, always use the full release name:

* Use: “What’s new in Ubuntu 14.04 LTS”
* Do not use: “What’s new in Ubuntu 14.04”

Referring to a product by its full name throughout a document can make the text seem clumsy and awkward. You only need to use the full product name on its first mention in a document, then a simplified version in the remaining text. Examples of this include:

| First mention | Second mention | Third mention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Ubuntu Server 21.04 | Ubuntu Server | Ubuntu |
| Ubuntu 21.04 | Ubuntu | N/A |
| Ubuntu Desktop 23.04 Lunar Lobster | Ubuntu Desktop or Lunar Lobster | N/A |
| Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (the long-term supported version of Ubuntu) Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS Ubuntu Desktop 22.04 LTS | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS | N/A |
| Ubuntu Server on Amazon EC2 | N/A | N/A |
| Ubuntu Core 24 | Ubuntu Core or Core 24  | N/A |

#### **Ubuntu Pro (formerly Ubuntu Advantage)**

Ubuntu Pro is Canonical’s comprehensive subscription for enterprise security, compliance and support.

When referring to Ubuntu Pro and its plans, please use the following conventions:

| Use this first | Later use this, if appropriate | Don’t use these |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Ubuntu Pro | Pro | Ubuntu Pro Apps |
| Ubuntu Pro (Infra-only) | Pro (Infra-only) | Ubuntu Pro Infrastructure UA for Infrastructure UA Infrastructure UA-I Pro infra |
| Ubuntu Pro + Support | N/A | Ubuntu support Ubuntu Pro support |
| Ubuntu Pro Desktop | Pro Desktop | N/A |
| Expanded Security Maintenance | ESM  | Extended Security Maintenance |

### Headings and capitalization

All headings and headlines should be sentence case. This means that you should only capitalize the first word.

* Use: Ubuntu reaches new heights
* Don't use: Ubuntu Reaches New Heights

You should only capitalize:

* product names (see section below for list of product names)
* personal names
* company names
* brands
* places
* Ubuntu Server, not Ubuntu server
* Ubuntu on phones, not Ubuntu Phone

If it is not the actual product name, it should not be capitalized. Never capitalize keywords, technical terms and jargon.

* Correct: “Ubuntu is great on the cloud”
* Incorrect: “Ubuntu is great on the Cloud”

* Correct: “Ubuntu Server is good for business”
* Incorrect: “Ubuntu server is good for business”

* Correct: “We are working alongside the University of Reading. The university is helping us in a research project.”
* Incorrect: “We are working alongside the University of Reading. The University is helping us in a research project.”

* Correct: “Ubuntu is the hyperscale leader in the cloud”
* Incorrect: “Ubuntu is the Hyperscale leader in the Cloud”

Job titles should only be capitalized when indicating a quote source.

* Correct: Luca Paulina, User Experience Designer, Canonical [as the source of a quote]
* Correct: Luca Paulina is a user experience designer [mid-sentence]

### Consistency

As we begin to establish common rules to follow across all Canonical communications, please try to stick to the following spellings:

* email
* online
* setup (noun), set up (verb)
* backup (noun), back up (verb)
* web
* website
* internet
* systems management
* virtualization
* multi-cloud
* whitepaper

* dos and don’ts

* on premises

If you don't have access to the style guide and you're having trouble remembering what our rules are, make sure that the spellings you use in a document are the same throughout. For example, if you begin a document referring to a website, every further reference should be the same.

### Dates

The correct date format across *.ubuntu.com and canonical.com sites is:

* Single day: January 1, 2013
* Date range within same month: January 1-2, 2013
* Date range across two or more months: January 1 - February 2,  2013

In technical material, please stick to the [ISO 8601 standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601) with “YYYY-MM-DD.”

Incorrect:

* 1st January 2013
* 01 January 2013
* 1 Jan 2013

Avoid slash dates (“dd/mm/yyyy” or “mm/dd/yyyy”) in written prose. They can be a source of confusion.

### Quotation marks

Quotations should include punctuation.

* Correct: Mark said “I like that,” and Matt said “I like that too.”
* Incorrect: Mark said “I like that”, and Matt said “I like that too”.

### Punctuation

#### **Exclamation marks**

Avoid exclamation marks on webpage copy. Use word choice rather than punctuation to evoke emotion. Feel free to use exclamation marks in blogs and other forms of copy.

#### **Question marks**

Always use a single question mark.

#### **Serial comma**

We use serial commas for lists in a sentence. We do try to simplify language and use bulleted lists when possible.

Example: Download Ubuntu to benefit from the latest UI improvements, enterprise features, and gaming enhancements.

### Links

Use links wisely: make sure every link you include has a context. “Click here” is meaningless. The link should indicate what users can expect to find when they click on the link. For accessibility reasons, we avoid using "Read more" and " See more" for hyperlinks. Use instead: “Learn more about Landscape.”

Do not use the verb “download” in buttons unless clicking on the button will automatically start the download. If it will not start the download, use the verb “get” instead.

Incorrect:

* Click here.
* See more.
* Read more.

Correct:

* Learn more about [Product/usecase].

### Units

There should not be a space between the value and the unit:

* Use: 3GB RAM
* Do not use: 3 GB RAM

Other common units:

* b
* KB
* MB
* GB
* TB
* GHz

## General best-practice guidelines

### Apostrophes

Apostrophes can be separated into two clear categories: to show possession and to show that one or more letters have been missed out. Most of the confusion seems to arise with possession.

The main rule is that if the name or noun is in the singular, add an apostrophe (') followed by the letter “s.” If the name or noun is a plural ending in “s,’ simply add an apostrophe.

* Use: The player's house was burgled.
* Use: The players' houses were burgled.

The exception to this rule is it's and its. Remember: it's = it is, its = belonging to it (the possessive).

Another common mistake is you're and your. Remember: you're = you are, your = belonging to you.

Take a look at the [Plurals and possessives](#plurals-and-possessives) section for guidelines on writing plural acronyms.

### Active sentences

A good way to keep sentences concise is to make them active rather than passive. Try to stick to a subject-verb-object sentence structure.

* Use: Fred joined the company today.
* Don't use: The company was joined by Fred today.

It's particularly important to keep your sentences simple when you're writing for the web. Just remember to get to the point, fast.

### Words and phrases to avoid

Try to avoid jargon, long-winded phrases and words with negative connotations. Steer clear of the following:

* Allow – This suggests that we are in a position of power, permitting users or customers to conduct certain activities.
* The ability to – Use “We can” instead of “We have the ability to”
* Is able to – Use “Ubuntu can” instead of “Ubuntu is able to”
* Not only...but also...
* Metal/Bare metal
* Eliminate
* Execute
* Terminate
* Kill
* Disruptive
* Explosive
* Leverage - Use “use” instead
* Going forward
* In order to
* Form factor
* End user – Use “user” instead

It can be tempting to use flowery, official-sounding words rather than plain English. Try to keep it simple.

### Code

Often the content you produce will have code in it. The code snippets (independent code chunks) can be formatted as follows:

````py
```code
model = tf.keras.models.Sequential([
  tf.keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=(28, 28)),
  tf.keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu'),
  tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.2),
  tf.keras.layers.Dense(10)
])
```endcode
````


#### **Code in text**

What happens when a code term comes within a sentence? Style your code term within the text as **bold**. A code term can be a variable, command, filename or any term from a larger code chunk. For example:

* Access the **index.html** file.
* The **run** command will allow you to directly open the application.


### Screentext

To bring your readers’ attention to a word/phrase within a screenshot, use the bold style.

For instance: **Learn more about Ubuntu Pro >**

### Emphasis (bold, italics and quotes)

Emphasis can change the meaning of sentences. It also helps in conveying your emotions to the readers. To effectively denote emphasis, you can use the bold, italics or quotes.

Use double quotes to include a coined term. Example: “Staycation” is the latest trend.

To emphasize a common word, use italics. Despite being birds, penguins *can’t* fly.

Use bold to highlight a word in a definition. Once defined, the same word must not be bolded again in the text.

Example: “A **Bayesian classifier** is a probabilistic model where the classification is a latent variable that is probabilistically related to the observed variables.”

### Tables

Tables of comparison, values of experiments or any data can be tricky to format. However, due to the visually appealing and crisp nature of tables, they can heavily improve the readability of your content. If used wisely, tables convey heaps of information and insights within a single block of content. Here’s how you can format tables:


Use bold for the table headings (row and column names).

Use normal text formatting for the content within the table.

### Acronyms and abbreviations

#### **Defining acronyms**

Assume nothing. Just because you know what ERP means, and the people you’ve discussed it with know what it means, it doesn’t follow that the majority of your audience knows. If you introduce unheard-of acronyms into your text without saying what they mean, your audience is likely to lose interest.

Spell out the acronym in full on its first mention in the document and include the acronym in brackets. After that, use the acronym exclusively. The only exceptions are acronyms in very common usage, for example BBC or IT.

Enterprise resource planning (ERP) is fine. But ERP makes the reader feel like they should already know what it means.

You can find out more about writing plural acronyms in the **Plurals and possessives** section.

#### **Latin abbreviations**

Avoid Latin abbreviations in **webpages**. Use “for example” or “meaning that” instead of “e.g.” or “i.e.,”. Use “and more” or “and others” instead of “etc.” In longform content (like whitepapers) use these abbreviations sparingly.

Note: the correct form of both ‘**e.g.,**’ and ‘**i.e.,**’ includes **two periods**, and **a comma** separating them from the text. However, they do not need to be italicised, despite being latin abbreviations. Ensure you’re using the right format of both - and consistently!

#### **Company names**

We also need to respect the full names of other companies. As a result, try to avoid unnecessary abbreviations and remember to never abbreviate “Microsoft” to “MSFT,” and “and” to “&.”

#### **Country names and supranational entity names**

For certain countries or supranational entities, it’s common to refer to them by an acronym, rather than their full name. For example, the United States as the US, the United Kingdom as the UK, or the European Union as the EU.

In these cases, do not add periods between the letters.  For example, it should always be “US,” not “U.S.”

If a country or entity is not commonly shortened to an acronym, you should not use an acronym and instead use the full name.

| Full name | Abbreviation | Avoid |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| European Union | EU | E.U |
| United Arab Emirates | UAE | U.A.E  |
| United Kingdom | UK | U.K, GB |
| United States | US | USA, U.S.A, U.S |
| United Nations | UN | U.N |

### Hyphens

Hyphens link words that form a composite adjective before a noun. Examples of adjectives formed from two or more words include:

* Best-practice processes
* Cloud-based
* Computer-based work
* Cost-effective
* Enterprise-ready
* Fully-featured
* High-availability
* High-quality services
* High-volume
* Real-time Ubuntu
* Real-time events (Real time is normally two words, unless it’s an adjective before a noun)
* Scale-out
* Short-term goals
* Third-party
* Three-year-old child
* Web-based
* 30-day subscription

The presence or absence of a hyphen can easily change the meaning. Compare: “The building has no smoking areas” to “The building has no-smoking areas.”

### En dash

The en dash (–) can be used in situations where you want to replace commas or parentheses for enhanced readability.

For example:

Upon discovering the vulnerabilities – all 20 of them – the company decided to look for a patch management solution.

#### **En dash vs em dash vs hyphen**

We use en dashes (–) rather than em dashes (—) to indicate breaks in a sentence. While grammatically, an em dash without spaces is technically correct, en dashes with spaces on either side look better visually. Never use a hyphen in place of a dash.

* Use: Upon discovering the vulnerabilities – all 20 of them – the company decided to look for a patch management solution.
* Don’t use:
  * Upon discovering the vulnerabilities—all 20 of them—the company decided to look for a patch management solution.
  * Upon discovering the vulnerabilities - all 20 of them - the company decided to look for a patch management solution.

### Numbers

Numbers in single figures should be spelled out in most cases. From 10 onwards, numbers should be written in digits.

Exceptions to this rule include numbered lists and units of measurement.

When writing out numbers over the 100s, remember to include commas.

* Use: 7,000
* Don't use: 7000

We use “24/7” not “24x7.”

### Plurals and possessives {#plurals-and-possessives}

Ubuntu and Canonical should both be referred to as singular entities.

For example, use “Canonical is” or “Canonical has,” not “Canonical are” or “Canonical have.”

Do not put apostrophes into decades or plural abbreviations.

* Use: The 1990s
* Don't use: The 1990's

* Use: Members of Parliament (MPs)
* Don't use: Members of Parliament (MP's)

* Use: Independent software vendors (ISVs)
* Don't use: Independent software vendors (ISV's)

However, phrases like “two weeks' time” and “six months' leave” do need apostrophes, because they are possessive.

### Lists

Bulleted lists make it easy for readers to scan content.

* Use capital letters for list items, even after a semicolon
* Use the same sentence structure for each bullet
* Do not use periods at the end of list items when all list items are one sentence or less

Use periods if any item on a bulleted list has more than one sentence. In this case, all items on the bulleted list should use a period – even list items with one sentence – for consistency. For example:

* 66% of experienced developers prefer Ubuntu. That’s why Ubuntu supports the fastest, biggest and most successful digital operations.
* Patch the full stack, from kernel to library and applications, for CVE compliance. Governments and auditors certify Ubuntu for FedRAMP, FISMA and HITECH.
* Companies engage Canonical to drive down open source operating costs.

**Line breaks**: Include a line break between the end of the bulleted list and the first paragraph of the next sentence.

### Superlatives

Don't try to add impact to your work by using superlatives you cannot justify. Make sure of your facts before you use words such as:

| unique | first | unprecedented |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| sole | only | last |
| exceptional | fastest | greatest |
| largest | smallest | heaviest |
| longest | tallest | record |
| slowest | least | matchless |
| exclusive | irreplaceable | most |
| inimitable |  |  |

Similarly, be sure to check your facts before using superlative phrases and use them sparingly:

| best in class | best of breed | top of the range |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| cutting edge | latest and greatest | state-of-the-art |
| one-of-a-kind | in a league of its own | in a class of its own |

### Capitalization of organizations

Random capitalization can interrupt the flow of a sentence and irritate the reader. As a general rule, you should only capitalize words when written in conjunction with a name or organization. Words like government, the administration and the cabinet should be lower case when on their own. Other examples include:

| First mention | Second mention |
| :---- | :---- |
| The University of Edinburgh | the university |
| The World Bank | the bank |
| The Welsh Assembly | the assembly |

## FAQs

There are some grammatical issues that can cause confusion. Here are some of the main offenders.

### What is the difference between fewer and less?

Fewer means “not as many,” less means “not as much.”

A commonly-quoted example used to highlight the distinction is: “There are fewer cars on the road, which means there is less traffic.”

Also compare: “The fewer people know about this the better” and “The less people know about this the better.”

Note: The rule does not work if the number is counted as a quantity or as a unit. For example: “She paid less than ten pounds for it” or “His last jump was less than fifteen feet.”

### What is the difference between that and which?

This can, and has, caused many arguments, so it's probably best not to get too worried about it. A useful guide is: that defines, which informs.

This is not a cast-iron rule but it can help: “This is the house that Jack built, but I think the one next door, which Jack also built, is more attractive.”

“Which” is often clausal, so is predominantly preceded by a comma.

Compare “The police stopped the second car that was driven by a woman” and “The police stopped the second car, which was driven by a woman.”

### Is it OK to split an infinitive?

There is no grammatical rule that says you can't split an infinitive. Sometimes, it is definitely better to split:

*Can dot.com companies ever hope to fully recover their share values?*

This sounds much better than moving “fully” in front of “to recover” or behind it. The key is not to write anything that is ambiguous or inelegant.
